extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in linguistics/semantics, humor studies, and performance analysis (e.g., scholars analyzing stand-up comedy and comedic texts)
extracted.subtask_description: A formal-semantic and pragmatic method for analyzing stand-up comedy jokes (transcribed performances), including categorizing comedic techniques, building real/imaginary ontologies, identifying performatives, and analyzing speaker intent via Gricean pragmatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign comedic category/categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign one or more comedic categories to a given joke (from the eleven types discussed elsewhere in the paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pre-established list of categories (points one to eleven). Examples in the text: character (2), reference (3), parody (5), shock, hyperbole (6), wordplay (7), madcap (9), physical/slapstick. A single joke can incorporate multiple categories (e.g., Bo’s rap uses character, reference, and parody).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and create ontology (real and imaginary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the state-of-affairs for the joke and construct its real ontology (ORe_S) and imaginary ontology (OIm_S), specifying extensions (E) and intensions/actions (I) for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List entities (E_Re, E_Im) and actions/relations (I_Re, I_Im) that constitute the performance; when the state-of-affairs evolves during performance, the ontology should reflect the whole performance (not necessarily separate ontologies for every shift). Examples: ORe_S for a stage performance includes BO, SPOTLIGHTS, MICROPHONE, AUDIENCE; OIm_S can include POLICE OFFICERS, HELICOPTER, SIRENS when those are imagined by the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the imaginary ontology as analyzable subset of state-of-affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: For analytic convenience, treat the imaginary ontology (retellings/fictional elements) as a subset of the state-of-affairs even though it is not 'technically' part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows consistent comparison between what is physically onstage and what is represented/imagined in the performance (e.g., police officers are placed in OIm_S rather than ORe_S because they are produced by lights/sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Map ontologies into a meta-language via formal semantic transformation (Fda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform the real and imaginary ontologies into meta-language counterparts (ORe_M, OIm_M) using the Fda mapping, producing N (nouns/entities) and P (predicates/actions) sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit N_Re, P_Re, N_Im, P_Im sets and predicate-argument relations (e.g., rap(cid:48) = {bo(cid:48)}; fall(cid:48) = {(bottle, stool)}). The paper uses this formal mapping to ground subsequent performative and pragmatic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and categorize performatives (Austinian approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the performatives being executed in the performance (e.g., rapping, singing, explaining, insulting) and attribute them to the appropriate ontology entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether performatives are properly invoked/executed (conditions for successful performance). Example: singing requires music; rapping is signaled by hip-hop music, body language, and audience participation. Divide performatives among characters when the performer plays multiple roles (e.g., BO_w and BO_m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose performative execution: misinvocation, misexecution, and abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether performatives are misinvoked, misexecuted, or abused, and treat such deviations as analytically significant (often contributing to humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bo’s lyrics (e.g., 'If you can divide by zero...') deviate from normal rap content (misinvocation); breaking established call-and-response conventions or switching to an unusually long audience response is 'abuse' of the performative; these deviations are explanatory mechanisms for why a bit is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze utterer’s intention and audience effect using Grice’s Cooperative Principle and maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the comedic exchange with Gricean variables (U = utterer, A = audience) and analyze intent/meaning in terms of adherence to or opt-out from the Cooperative Principle and its maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume U intends A to laugh (default) but analyze where U opts out of cooperative behavior (e.g., violating the maxim of Relation by asking irrelevant questions) and how opt-outs, 'gotcha' moments, or deceptive framing (e.g., mock-arrest prank) produce comedic effects. Use explicit examples from the transcript (lines cited) where U first follows and then opts out of cooperative expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Gricean notation and formalization for exchange modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent comedic interactions formally (e.g., U = Bo Burnham, A = audience, x2 = some joke, r = laughing) to tie intention to observable reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal notation supports claims like: by saying some joke, U intends A to laugh. The paper treats Cooperative Principle and maxims as followed by default unless analysable opt-outs are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcription standards for analytic adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribe performances including essential elements to support formal analysis: timestamps, line numbers, stage actions, speaker labels, sung vs spoken distinctions, audience responses, and non-verbal cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use square brackets for stage actions, bold for speaker names, italic for quoted speech, musical notation markers for lyrics, and include pauses, lighting/music changes, and audience laughter. Base transcriptions on show subtitles and independent sources to minimize inaccuracies (example transcription format provided in appendix D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for sample jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Select jokes to maximize diversity in performance style and content and to represent as many of the predefined categories as possible; exclude jokes where meaning cannot be explicitly defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selected sample in the study includes songs, physical routines, fictional stories, and aims to cover many of the eleven categories. Note: category δ (unspecified) is excluded because meaning tied to an implicitly unstated joke cannot be defined for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include staging and multimodal signals as analytic evidence of character/genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat lighting, music, body language, and audience participation as signals that assign roles/genres (e.g., rapper vs singer) and as elements of the ontology and performatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: purple/blue lights and hip-hop music mark the rapper character; soft blue light and piano indicate singer/girlfriend. These cues justify attributing character and genre-specific performatives and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain humor mechanisms in terms of expectation violation and genre convention manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify humor-generating mechanisms such as betrayal of audience expectations, opting out of cooperative norms, parody by blending roles, and using abnormal subject matter for a genre (misuse of standard practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples: Bo parodying rap by rapping about dividing by zero; abandoning call-and-response expectations to create 'gotcha' moments; flipping maturity roles between BO_w and BO_m. These are presented as reasons why particular jokes are funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle audience membership across ontologies (real/implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: When imaginary characters reference audience members, include the audience in predicate relations of the imaginary ontology even if they are formally part of the real ontology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: police-ofﬁcers in OIm_S1 'arrest' audience members who previously shouted 'Hell, yeah!'; hence audience appears in P_Im predicates though listed in E_Re.
